The snow globe struck the marble floor and shattered, and the word died with him. Alone in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, among the endless mirrors he'd commissioned to catch light that never quite arrived, Emmett Rusk let out his last breath with the word "Bluebell" on his lips. The butler Colm found him there the next morning, slumped in the chair where he'd sat for three days running, the glass fragments scattered like ice across the stone.

The newsreel obituary played in theaters across the state that week. It showed Emmett in his prime, shaking hands with governors, standing before the Clarion building, embracing Adele on the night of their engagement after a buying trip abroad. It showed him losing the governor's race, it showed his second marriage, it showed the slow strangulation of his reputation. It closed without explaining his last word, and the studio appended a card asking whether anyone in the audience knew what Bluebell meant.

The Clarion's last editor sent a reporter named Nash to find out.

Nash began where any man would, with the paper trail. He read Barrow's memoir, that dry and self-justifying document, and learned what no newsreel had mentioned: how Emmett's mother had signed her son over to the banker Barrow in a mining boarding house out west, after a defaulted lodger's mine deed made the family rich overnight. How the boy had driven his sled into Barrow's stomach in the yard, and how Barrow had taken him east anyway, away from his parents, away from the sled whose name he'd painted in blue letters on the runner: Bluebell.

Nash interviewed Marsh, who had managed Emmett's affairs for twenty years. Marsh told him about Emmett's twenty-fifth birthday, when the boy took control of the fortune and told Barrow that of all his holdings he wanted to run a failing city newspaper. How Emmett had moved into the Clarion, installed Marsh and his friend Devlin, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. How he'd hired away the entire staff of the rival paper and thrown a party with a brass band and a chorus line, as if journalism were something you could win by volume.

Nash interviewed Devlin, who was drinking in a bar in another city by then. Devlin told him about the breakfast-table scenes, the marriage to Adele cooling into silence behind separate newspapers. How Emmett had met the shopgirl Nora Kell on the street with mud on his coat and started visiting her rooms in secret. How the party boss Halloran had brought Adele to Nora's rooms mid-campaign and threatened exposure, and Emmett had refused to withdraw. How he'd lost the election, Devlin had asked for a transfer, and the marriage had collapsed.

Devlin told him about the second marriage. How Emmett had forced Nora into an opera career for which she had no voice. How her debut had been a humiliation, and how Devlin, drunk, had begun the savage review that Emmett finished, printed, and fired him for. How Nora had swallowed poison rather than sing again, and how Emmett had finally let her stop.

Nash interviewed Colm, who described the jigsaw puzzles. After the poison, Emmett had shut Nora away in Silvermount, where she worked puzzles in the vast empty hall, fitting pieces together that never formed a complete picture. After a joyless beach picnic and a quarrel, she had packed and left him. Emmett had wrecked her bedroom, found a glass snow globe, murmured "Bluebell," and carried it past the endless mirrors.

Nash found Nora in a seaside nightclub, drunk, and she turned him away at the door.

He stood on the boardwalk afterward with his notes in his pocket and watched the waves. Barrow's memoir, Marsh's ledgers, Devlin's bitterness, Colm's quiet loyalty, Nora's refusal. He had every piece now, and none of them fit together. No single word explains a life, he wrote that night, and filed the story.

At Silvermount, the workmen were clearing out the debris. They found the sled in a storage room beneath the stairs, the blue paint faded but the name still legible. They shoveled it into the furnace with the rest, and the fire took it, and the word burned away, and the light it made was brief.

The robbery collapsed inside sixty seconds. Sirens were on them before Mr. Ash had even pulled the getaway car to the curb, and Mr. Elm watched through the rear window as Ash leaned out and fired three controlled bursts that sent uniforms scrambling behind their cruisers. Ash swung the wheel hard and the city blurred past, Elm braced against the door, his cover story already fraying at the edges.

He thought of Pruitt, his handler, standing with him in that same car park for three nights running, making him tell the fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet until the words lost their scripted feel and settled into his mouth like something he'd actually lived. He thought of performing it for Bram and Cal and Mr. Ash in the back room of the club, the way Bram had studied him, the way Ash had laughed at the right moment, and the nod that followed—Danny Roarke erased, Mr. Elm born.

On foot now, fleeing through a rail yard, Elm flagged down a sedan and dragged the driver out. The man fought. A revolver appeared from somewhere—gripped in shaking, civilian hands—and a round punched into Elm's stomach just below the ribs. He fired back. The driver dropped and did not move again, and Elm stood over him, bleeding, the pain arriving in a white sheet that folded him nearly in half.

Ash found him stumbling along the access road. He pulled Elm into the car and drove fast, one hand on the wheel, the other pressing a wadded jacket to the wound. "You're not going to die," Ash said, and Elm wanted to believe him, not as a cop believing a suspect, but as a man believing a friend.

At the warehouse Ash half-carried him inside. The pain was enormous and specific. Elm remembered breakfast that morning, the crew arguing about what a pop song was really about, whether the waitress deserved a tip. He remembered Bram handing out the tree aliases—Mr. Birch objecting to being Mr. Birch, the small ridiculous protest—and Ren Vasco walking in that same morning, fresh from prison, blinking in the light, collecting on the years he'd kept his mouth shut. All of it felt like something that had happened to someone else.

Mr. Birch arrived next, agitated, convinced the job had been a setup. He argued there was an informer inside the crew, then took the diamonds and hid them outside the building without waiting for consensus.

Mr. Cedar strolled in after him. He popped the boot of his car and produced a kidnapped patrolman named Doyle, bound and gagged, and dumped him on the warehouse floor. Left alone with the officer, Cedar turned a radio to an oldie and danced to it, loose-limbed and grinning, before he cut off Doyle's ear and doused him in petrol from a jerry can.

Elm fired from where he lay on the concrete. Cedar dropped. Elm told Doyle he was a cop, that the police were waiting outside for Bram, that it would be over soon.

Cal returned. He listened to Elm's account of Cedar, looked at the body, looked at Doyle, and shot the patrolman dead himself.

Then Bram came through the door and named Mr. Elm as the informer. Ash refused to believe it. He turned his gun on Bram. Cal raised his. The warehouse went silent except for the radio still playing, and then it wasn't silent anymore.

When the echo cleared, Bram and Cal were down. Ash was down too but breathing, and Elm lay in a spreading warmth that he understood was not warmth at all.

He confessed. He told Ash he was a police officer. Ash looked at him with something that was not surprise and not betrayal but some third thing Elm had no name for, and then Ash raised his weapon and fired, and Elm felt the impact arrive very late, and the doors came in and the warehouse filled with uniforms and Ash was cut down in the crossfire, still pointing his gun at no one and everyone, and the oldie on the radio played on to its end.

The beach party was at the end of the rail line, the last stop, where the tracks gave up and the sea began. Tobias met Ivy there among the bonfires and someone's portable radio, and when the party thinned they broke into an empty house on the shore and sat with their feet in the dark and talked until dawn.

Later—months later, years—they sat in Ivy's flat with a cassette player between them, listening to their own recorded voices say things no one should have to hear. She ran. She came back. They agreed to try anyway, and the agreement was its own kind of wreckage, but they shook on it like strangers closing a deal.

He fell in love with her slowly, the way you fall into a frozen river—through the ice first, then all at once. The noodle house on Tuesdays. The drive-in in summer. Two years of accumulating a shared vocabulary of places and habits and private jokes that would become, eventually, a kind of language only two people spoke.

Rosa quit the clinic on a Thursday. She boxed the files, the session tapes, the intake forms, and mailed them all back—every patient on the books—because she believed, or wanted to believe, that people deserved to know what had been taken from them.

Then the language curdled. Recrimination over her drinking. Recrimination over his withholding. The same arguments rotating like dishes on a lazy Susan, each pass a little colder.

They drove back to the city together, the heater rattling, and she invited him up to her flat, and he followed because following was what he knew how to do.

She came home drunk with a dent in his fender and the fight that followed was not a fight but an ending. She walked out and the door closed behind her with the polite click of a door that knows it will not be opened again.

He skipped work on an impulse he could not account for. He took the train to the coast—the same line, the same last stop—and found her on the frozen sand, waiting as though she had always known he would come.

Ivy hired a clinic. She signed the forms, submitted to the mapping, and woke one morning with a space in her mind where Tobias had been, a space that felt not empty but natural, like a room that had always been spare.

Tobias woke the next morning and did not know anyone named Ivy. The flat was quiet. The light was ordinary. He felt rested and slightly sad and could not say why.

He found her in the bookshop on Creswell Street, treating him as a stranger, flirting with a young man behind the counter—a kid named Peck—and when he said her name she only smiled and asked if they'd met before.

In the last surviving memory, the empty house on the shore, they stood together one final time. She told him to meet her at the beach. He said okay. The walls went white around them.

Nina and Grady showed him the form letter from the clinic, and he went to Dr. Hallam and demanded the same procedure, his voice steady, his hands not.

Dr. Hallam arrived to re-map the erasure, and Rosa kissed him in the doorway—only for his wife to appear behind them both and reveal, with the calm of someone delivering a weather report, that Rosa's own affair with Hallam had been erased from her mind. She had loved him. She had paid to forget. Now she remembered only the forgetting.

He boxed up every object connected with Ivy—the mug she'd bought him, the scarf, the photograph from the drive-in—so the clinic could map the memories attached to them. He labeled each box. He was methodical. He was preparing to lose everything and he wanted the loss to be clean.

Dell and the receptionist Rosa got high on Tobias's bed and lost track of the procedure as his map went off the rails, the connections firing in wrong directions, memories bleeding into one another like watercolors in rain.

The technicians Dell and Peck ran the overnight erasure in his flat, and Peck pocketed the mementos to use on Ivy later—whatever later meant to a boy who collected other people's love like coins from a fountain.

Inside his own head, Tobias reached the memories he loved and changed his mind. He tried to smuggle Ivy into memories she was never part of—a childhood birthday, a train ride alone—hiding her in the corners like a stowaway on a ship that was already sinking

He went to support groups for diseases he did not have—bone marrow failure, parasitic trematodes, blood clotting disorders—and wept in the circle of folding chairs until exhaustion finally dragged him under. He was a product-recall investigator. He did not sleep. Then he slept, briefly, and it was enough.

He would later put a gun in his own mouth in a tower stairwell and pull the trigger, the bullet passing through his cheek, and Rex would slump against the wall with him, sharing the same ruined face, finally still. But he did not know that yet.

What he knew was that Ada Vey started attending the same groups, and her obvious faking destroyed his release. She chewed her lip too theatrically. She wore her suffering like a brooch. He could not cry in front of her. The insomnia came back.

On a business flight he met a soap salesman named Rex Marrow, who handed him a card with a winking grin, and he pocketed it without thinking. Weeks later his flat and all his catalogue furniture were destroyed in an explosion, and he called Rex from the rubble. Rex took him to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district, where the wallpaper hung in long tongues and the kitchen smelled of lye.

Outside a bar Rex asked him to hit him as hard as he could. The two beat each other bloody in the car park, and something cracked open in both of them—or in one of them—that could not be closed again. What started as two men brawling hardened into a weekly basement club with its own rules, pulling in more and more members. Ada overdosed. Rex brought her back to the derelict house, and the two began a loud affair the narrator could not stand, the sounds carrying through the rotting walls at night.

Rex rendered fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap and sold it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He burned the narrator's hand with lye and held him there, refusing to let him retreat into meditation, the chemical kiss eating through to the bone. The narrator blackmails his employer into paying him to stay away, using his own beaten face as the evidence. Rex turned the club into an organisation he called Havoc, filling the house with shaven recruits who took orders and vandalise corporate property.

At a window in one of the towers, Ada would hold his hand and the buildings would come down, and it would look like freedom. But he did not know that yet either.

Rex steered the car into oncoming traffic, let it roll, and then disappeared. A member of Havoc named Ogden was shot dead on an operation, and the narrator started trying to shut the whole thing down. Travelling city to city, he found identical clubs everywhere and men who greeted him as Rex Marrow. The narrator worked out that he and Rex were the same person, and that Rex had been acting while he slept. Ada confirmed that she had been sleeping with him, not with a separate man.

He discovered that Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies and tried to defuse the charges. Rex beat him down a stairwell in one of the towers, and the narrator put a gun in his own mouth and shot himself through the cheek to kill Rex. The body that was both of them crumpled on the landing, and for the first time in years the narrator felt only one will inside him, only one set of hands.

Ada was delivered to the tower by the shaven recruits. She found him bleeding at the window. She took his hand. The buildings came down, and it looked like freedom.

In a flat overlooking the street, an old man was explaining to a younger one that nothing survives time. Below them, blue lights strobed across wet pavement and two figures were being carried out of a club in handcuffs.

The police loaded Cort and Jonah into separate cars. Cort's arm hung at a wrong angle, the skin above the elbow already purpling. Jonah's knuckles were split open, smeared with someone else's blood. Neither of them spoke. The doors shut. The cars pulled away.

Minutes before, Jonah had been swinging a fire extinguisher into a man's face—again, again—while the real Adder stood a few feet away, watching with the mild curiosity of someone observing weather. Cort was on his knees, cradling his snapped arm, the wrong man's shirt still bunched in his fist. He had seized the wrong man. He had been sure. The Adder smiled thinly and slipped into the crowd.

They had come here because two men in the street had offered to sell Cort the rapist's name. The men had leaned into the ambulance's wake, speaking low and fast, steering Cort and Jonah toward a place called the Pit. Cort had gone rigid with purpose. Jonah had followed because that was what Jonah did.

Before the club, before the street, they had come out of the party and found Lise being loaded into the ambulance on a stretcher. Her face was unrecognizable. Cort had screamed her name and Jonah had grabbed the paramedic's sleeve and neither of them had been able to follow her inside.

What had happened to her in the underpass was this: the Adder had been beating a transsexual woman when Lise walked in. Lise had turned to run. He had caught her. He had raped her on the concrete and then he had beaten her head against the floor, methodically, as though seasoning a cut of meat. A passer-by had glimpsed them from the stairwell and backed away into the night.

Lise had taken the underpass because she did not want to cross the busy road. She had left the party on her own because Cort had gotten steadily drunk and high and started pursuing other women, leaning into them with his loose, grinning confidence, his hand on a stranger's hip. Lise had watched from across the room, disgusted, and then she had simply walked out.

The party had started on the underground. Lise, Cort, and Jonah had ridden together in a rattling carriage, arguing cheerfully about sex and about Cort's drinking. Jonah had said Cort couldn't handle his liquor and Cort had said Jonah couldn't handle anything and Lise had laughed between them, the three of them compressed into a kind of warmth that would not survive the evening.

Before the party, before the underground, Lise had sat in a park reading among sprinklers and playing children, one hand resting on her stomach. She had not told Cort yet. She had not told anyone. The positive test was still wrapped in tissue at the bottom of the bathroom bin, two pink lines fading behind a white plastic window.

She had taken the pregnancy test alone in the flat while Cort was out. She had sat on the edge of the bathtub and waited the full three minutes, watching the control line appear and then the second one, faint at first, then undeniable. She had held it under the light. She had breathed.

And before that—before the test, before the park, before any of it—she had lain in bed with Cort describing a recurring dream of a red tunnel. She told him how the walls pressed close and warm, how the light at the end pulsed like a heartbeat, how she always woke before reaching it. Cort had traced a line down her ribs and said it sounded like she was afraid of being born. She had said maybe she was afraid of being born again. They had teased each other about Jonah, her ex, who still texted her sometimes, who still showed up at the same pubs. Cort had said Jonah was the kind of man who confused persistence with devotion. Lise had said at least Jonah remembered her birthday. Cort had pulled her closer and said he didn't need a calendar to know what mattered.

She had closed her eyes and the red tunnel had been there, waiting, as it always was, patient and dim.

Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, were getting ready for a dinner party across town. Bess stood before the mirror in a slip, dabbing perfume behind her ears, while Neil straightened his tie and checked his watch twice.

That same morning the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake—a boy called Charlie Rill, turning eight. Otto wrote the name carefully in his ledger, though no one had paid him for the last three orders and the shop's phone had been disconnected for non-payment. He boxed up a receipt and slid it beneath the till.

Charlie was knocked down by a car on his way to school. The driver, a waitress called Rhona, ran to him in the road, but Charlie stood, brushed the dirt from his knees, and walked home insisting he was fine. His mother Elaine cleaned the graze on his elbow. His father Grant let him lie on the sofa with a comic. By afternoon Charlie's eyes had rolled back and he collapsed into a coma, and his parents kept vigil at the hospital, taking turns pressing his warm fingers.

Grant's estranged father Duff turned up that evening, smelling of cigarettes and road dust. He sat in the corridor and confessed an affair from decades ago, weeping into his hands, while Grant stared at the wall above the old man's head.

Unpaid and ignored, the baker began making anonymous menacing phone calls to the family from a payphone on the corner, breathing into the receiver, then whispering threats he didn't mean.

Across town, telephone-sex worker Cheryl talked men through their fantasies from her living room, her voice low and practised, while her husband Stu seethed beside her on the sofa, watching football with the sound off. The next morning Stu and three friends drove out to fish and found a young woman's body face down in the river. The men tethered the body to the bank with a length of rope and carried on fishing for two more days before telling anyone. When Vern's wife Iris, a party clown, learned what the men had done, she was disgusted. She packed Vern's clothes into a bin liner and left it on the porch.

The singer Vida performed nightly in a club downtown, her voice carrying over the clink of glasses, while her cellist daughter Bee played alone at home in an empty house.

Officer Rowe, cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan, abandoned the family dog in a parking lot to cover one of his lies. Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had a new man and sawed her furniture to pieces in her driveway while she watched from the window.

Ike and Dot house-sat for the Hartigans and photographed Dot made up as a beaten corpse, the Polaroids curling on the kitchen counter.

At the dinner party Bess admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and an affair, and Neil made a scene, knocking his wine glass into the centrepiece.

Charlie died in hospital. Grant and Elaine went to the bakery to confront Otto, who fed them warm bread and grieved with them, weeping freely, his floury hands trembling.

Bee found her mother asleep on the sofa, still in her stage dress. She closed the garage door and killed herself with the car engine running.

At a picnic in the hills, Stu smashed a young woman's head with a rock.

A tremor shook the entire city, and every death and every wreck was folded into one evening bulletin, read by a woman whose voice never broke.

Emlyn said he had known for four years. His wife had told him on the trip abroad, he said, standing in Wilder's hallway with his coat still on. And he had never thought much of his friend's letters either. Wilder stood in the doorway of his own front room, unable to sit down, unable to ask Emlyn to sit, and the words landed with the dull weight of things that had been true for a long time. Four years. The whole life of the rented rooms and everything after, Emlyn had carried the knowledge like a coin in a pocket he never turned out.

Wilder had rung him in a state. That much Wilder could remember clearly — the receiver hot against his ear, the fumbling through Emlyn's number, the surprise of how quickly Emlyn agreed to come. It had been Odile's doing, indirectly. In a bar, two years after everything, she had told him her marriage was over, that she had spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband at last, as though it were news. And then she had let slip, almost carelessly, that Emlyn had been publishing a writer whom Wilder represented — a writer both men quietly detested. The information sat in Wilder's chest like a stone. He could not leave it. He picked up the phone.

But Odile's confession, it turned out, was not a confession at all. Emlyn had known since the hotel abroad, since the afternoon at the desk when he asked about a letter held for her, addressed in a hand he recognised. She had confessed then, on that foreign carpet, in that strange light, and Emlyn had remarked — with what Wilder imagined was the same calm he showed tonight — that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife.

Wilder tried to reconstruct the sequence. After the trip, Odile had come back to the rented rooms and said nothing about it. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had. She set the kettle on. She moved the cups. Wilder had not asked, and she had not offered, and the rooms held their quiet arrangement as though nothing in the wider world had shifted.

Before the trip, there had been the long restaurant lunch. Emlyn drinking through it, baiting Wilder about contemporary fiction, never once mentioning what he had learned. Wilder had thought Emlyn was merely drunk and disagreeable. He had not understood that Emlyn was enjoying something.

And before the lunch, the dinner at the married couple's house. The two men discussing racquet games and schoolboy sport until Odile had no part in the talk at all. Wilder had thought she looked tired. He had not considered that Emlyn was performing something for her benefit — showing her how easily he and Wilder could carry on, how little the affair had disturbed the surface between men.

Before all of that, the rooms. Wilder and Odile renting them in a quiet district, filling them with linen and plates, giving the affair a household of its own. Then Odile saying she was carrying her husband's child, and the pair deciding the rooms would go on exactly as before. And they had. For a while. Until the rooms became a chore and they split the crockery and surrendered the lease, packing the last of the cups into separate boxes, neither of them crying.

And before the rooms, the beginning. A party at the house of Emlyn — his closest friend, whose wife stood at the foot of the stairs holding a glass while Wilder led Odile to an upstairs room and told her how lovely she was. The other guests drank below. Music came up through the floor. Odile had looked at him with an expression he had taken for invitation and was, he now understood, something else entirely — perhaps the look of someone who already knew the marriage was hollow and was searching for proof.

Emlyn was still standing in the hallway. He had not moved to leave. He had not moved to sit. He looked at Wilder with what might have been pity, or might have been the last residue of a fondness he claimed to have felt for years, and Wilder understood that the friendship had been the thing Emlyn mourned least and wielded most.

Solly Two Coats had a gift for disguise. He and his crew dressed as devout pilgrims, humble and mute, and walked into the diamond house in the northern port with heads bowed and hands folded. They walked out with a stone the size of a robin's egg, and no one raised a voice until they were long gone.

Word reached his cousin Marv overseas. Marv sent a message back: bring the stone straight over, no stops, no nonsense.

But Solly never could resist nonsense. Grigor the Nail found him first, told him about a bookmaker's in the city where the odds were sweet on a fixed fight. Grigor, in the same breath, tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to be at that bookmaker's when Solly arrived with his case.

The fight had its own machinery grinding away. Boxing promoters Halloway and Digby had sent the fighter Pretty Sam to a camp of travellers to buy a caravan for training quarters. Sam made the mistake of haggling with the wrong man. The bare-knuckle fighter Finn knocked him cold over the deal, and suddenly Halloway had no man for the bout he'd promised to fix for the gang boss Coldstone.

Halloway went to Coldstone and promised that Finn would go down in the fourth round. It was the only card he had left.

Solly landed in the city and delivered the stone to the fence Hersch, who counted out the money without a word. Then Solly headed for the bookmaker's, case under his good arm, to lay a bet on the fight.

Ike, Benno and a man named Tulley were waiting. They bungled the robbery badly, took Solly's arm and his case both, and might have done worse if Grigor hadn't come round the corner and chased them off. Solly staggered away bleeding.

At the ring, Finn knocked his opponent out cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and took it out of Halloway with his fists.

Marv flew in, found Solly gone from the hotel, and hired the bounty hunter Ledge to find him.

Grigor found Solly first. He cut off the ruined arm to get the case open and found nothing inside. The stone was not there.

Ledge traced the pawnbrokers. He shot their car to pieces on the road and took both Ike and Benno, and the stone along with them.

Coldstone fed Solly to his pigs. He told Halloway and Digby what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong.

They told Finn to go down in the fourth. And Coldstone's men went to the travellers' camp and burned Finn's mother to death in her caravan to make sure the message was understood.

Grigor ambushed Ledge's car on the road, Ike and Benno still inside. In the shootout Ledge, Grigor and Benno were all killed. Tulley, who had been following at a distance, got away with the dog that had swallowed the diamond.

Finn stepped into the ring for the second fight. In the fourth round he knocked his opponent out again, and the travellers, scattered through the crowd, opened fire on Coldstone's men. It was a slaughter.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone in the chaos and shot him. By morning the travellers had vanished from the city like smoke.

The dog wandered the streets for days until someone handed it in at a pet shop. It coughed up the diamond on the floor among the parakeets and hamsters. The stone rolled to a stop, and before the day was out Halloway and Digby had come to claim it, and they sat holding it between them like men who had forgotten what it was ever worth.

He has always known he will be shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd. He knows this the way a person knows anything — which is to say, he believes it, and belief is the only architecture a moment has.

He is a boy born in a small industrial town, a weak and peculiar child. His father throws him into the deep end of a pool. He sinks to the bottom and rests there, looking up at the light broken on the surface, and the light is not different from any other light he will see. He is conscripted as a chaplain's assistant and shipped overseas with no training worth the name. He is lost behind the lines with a scout who beats him for wanting to be left to die. The pair are captured. The scout dies of gangrene on the prison train, blaming him with his last breath, and the breath is just air, and the air does not care who used it first.

He is held in a camp beside enemy officers who have been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error. The error is nobody's fault. The rations taste like rations. He is sent on to a great city and housed with other prisoners in a disused abattoir. The city is destroyed by fire in one night. The prisoners in the meat locker come up to find it gone. They are made to dig bodies out of the cellars until one of the diggers dies of the dry heaves. A fellow prisoner promises to have him killed one day on the dead scout's account.

He comes home, collapses, and is hospitalised. Another patient introduces him to a hack science fiction writer. He marries the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school and becomes rich. He survives an air crash in the mountains. His wife dies of exhaust fumes driving to the hospital. He is taken by aliens and kept in a zoo on their planet with a film actress. The aliens explain that every moment exists at once and that free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet.

He goes on a radio talk show and tries to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension. His daughter decides he is senile and takes his affairs out of his hands.

Every moment exists at once. This is what the aliens tell him, and he believes them, and believing is the only thing he does, the only thing anyone does, because free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet and his planet is not peculiar in any way that matters.

He sinks to the bottom of the pool. He digs bodies out of cellars. He stands in a zoo on a planet that is not his. He addresses a crowd. He marries. He is beaten. He rests in the meat locker. He is rich. He is shot dead. He is a boy. He is a chaplain's assistant. He is an optometrist. He is a prisoner. He is a husband. He is a zoo exhibit. He is a son. He is a corpse being dug out of a cellar by someone who will die of the dry heaves. He is a voice on the radio. He is a child resting at the bottom of a pool, looking up at the light.

The light does not change.

The scout blames him with his last breath. His wife drives to the hospital. The aliens explain. His father throws. The city burns. His daughter takes his affairs. The beam weapon fires. The clerical error feeds the officers. The film actress is beside him in the zoo. The hack writer is introduced. The air crash happens. The pool holds him. The train carries the gangrene. The crowd listens. The rations are doubled. The meat locker is cold. The bottom of the pool is quiet.

Every moment exists at once. He is shot dead after addressing a crowd, exactly as he has always known he would be. He sinks to the bottom. He comes home. He is born. He is rich. He is peculiar. He is weak. He is a boy in an industrial town. He is an old man on a radio talk show. He is a prisoner in a disused abattoir. He is none of these things in any order, because there is no order, because order is an idea peculiar to his own planet, and his planet is on fire, and the fire is not different from any other fire, and the light does not change.
